Acne vulgaris: A common skin condition characterized by the presence of comedones, papules, pustules, and sometimes nodules or cysts, typically caused by inflammation and blockage of hair follicles and sebaceous glands. 2. Acne rosacea: A chronic inflammatory skin disorder primarily affecting the central face, presenting with erythema, telangiectasia, papules, and pustules, often triggered by environmental or dietary factors. 3. Anthrax, cutaneous: A bacterial infection caused by Bacillus anthracis, presenting as a painless papule that progresses to a vesicle and then a necrotic ulcer with a characteristic black eschar. 4. Bacillary angiomatosis: A vascular proliferative disease caused by Bartonella species, often seen in immunocompromised individuals, presenting as red to purple papules or nodules that may ulcerate. 5. Bite wounds: Injuries caused by animal or human bites, often complicated by polymicrobial infections, requiring thorough cleaning, debridement, and appropriate antibiotic therapy. 6. Carbuncle: A deep, interconnected cluster of furuncles (boils) caused by bacterial infection, typically Staphylococcus aureus, presenting as a painful, swollen, and erythematous mass with purulent drainage. 7. Cat scratch disease: A bacterial infection caused by Bartonella henselae, typically following a scratch or bite from a cat, presenting with regional lymphadenopathy and sometimes systemic symptoms. 8. Cellulitis: A bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, presenting with erythema, warmth, swelling, and tenderness, often caused by Streptococcus or Staphylococcus species. 9. Ecthyma: A deeper form of impetigo caused by bacterial infection, presenting as ulcerative lesions with a thick crust, often associated with poor hygiene or immunosuppression. 10. Erysipelas: A superficial bacterial skin infection involving the upper dermis, presenting with well-demarcated, raised, erythematous plaques, commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes. 11. Erysipeloid: A bacterial infection caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, often seen in individuals handling fish or meat, presenting with localized, painful, and violaceous skin lesions. 12. Erythrasma: A superficial bacterial infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum, presenting as well-demarcated, reddish-brown patches, often in intertriginous areas, with a characteristic coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp. 13. Furuncle: A bacterial infection of a hair follicle and surrounding tissue, presenting as a painful, erythematous nodule with purulent drainage, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. 14. Gas gangrene: A life-threatening infection caused by Clostridium species, characterized by rapid tissue necrosis, gas production, severe pain, and systemic toxicity. 15. Glanders: A rare bacterial infection caused by Burkholderia mallei, primarily affecting animals but transmissible to humans, presenting with ulcerative skin lesions, fever, and systemic involvement. 16. Impetigo: A superficial bacterial skin infection, often caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, presenting with honey-colored crusted lesions. Adult treatment: For a limited number of lesions, topical mupirocin or retapamulin applied twice daily for 5 days is preferred. For numerous lesions or outbreaks, oral antibiotics such as dicloxacillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or cephalexin for 7 days are recommended. For penicillin-allergic patients, alternatives include doxycycline, clindamycin, or sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. If culture confirms Streptococcus alone, penicillin V is preferred, with erythromycin or clindamycin as alternatives for penicillin-allergic patients. For methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), doxycycline, clindamycin, or sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim are preferred. Pediatric treatment: For a limited number of lesions, topical mupirocin or retapamulin applied twice daily for 5 days is preferred. For numerous lesions or outbreaks, oral antibiotics such as amoxicillin-clavulanate or cephalexin for 7 days are recommended. For penicillin-allergic patients, alternatives include clindamycin or sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. If culture confirms Streptococcus alone, penicillin V is preferred, with erythromycin or clindamycin as alternatives for penicillin-allergic patients. For MRSA, clindamycin or sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim are preferred. 17. Lyme disease, cutaneous: A tick-borne infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi, presenting with erythema migrans, a characteristic expanding red rash with central clearing. 18. Mastitis: Inflammation of the breast tissue, often associated with lactation, presenting with localized pain, erythema, swelling, and sometimes systemic symptoms, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. 19. Necrotizing fasciitis: A rapidly progressive, life-threatening soft tissue infection involving the fascia, characterized by severe pain, erythema, swelling, and systemic toxicity, often requiring surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics. 20. Pilonidal cyst: A chronic infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue near the coccyx, presenting with pain, swelling, and purulent drainage, often requiring surgical intervention. 21. Pyomyositis: A bacterial infection of skeletal muscle, presenting with localized pain, swelling, fever, and abscess formation, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. 22. Seborrheic dermatitis: A chronic inflammatory skin condition affecting sebaceous gland-rich areas, presenting with erythematous, scaly patches, and dandruff, often associated with Malassezia species. 23. Surgical site infections: Infections occurring at or near a surgical incision site, presenting with erythema, swelling, pain, and purulent drainage, often caused by Staphylococcus aureus or other skin flora. 24. Vascular insufficiency ulcer: Chronic wounds caused by poor blood flow, presenting with non-healing ulcers, often on the lower extremities, requiring wound care and management of underlying vascular disease. 25. Yaws: A chronic bacterial infection caused by Treponema pallidum pertenue, presenting with skin lesions that progress from papillomas to ulcers, primarily affecting children in tropical regions.
